query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a ductile metallic binder phase, such as aluminum (Al), into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy will enhance mechanical integrity (e.g., increase compressive strength and reduce cracking) without significantly compromising its caloric response.
generation.intervention: Introduce a ductile metallic binder phase (e.g., aluminum) into the alloy matrix.
generation.conditions: Applied magnetic field up to 2 T, pressure field up to 100 MPa, temperature range of 200–400 K, and compressive loading up to 200 MPa.
generation.structural_mediator: The ductile metallic binder phase will distribute stress more evenly across the alloy matrix, reducing crack propagation and improving mechanical integrity.
generation.mechanism: The ductile metallic binder phase will act as a stress-relief medium, absorbing and redistributing mechanical loads while maintaining sufficient thermal and magnetic coupling to preserve the caloric response.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit a compressive strength increase of at least 50% compared to the unmodified alloy, with no more than a 10% reduction in caloric response under the specified conditions.
generation.baseline: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which has poor mechanical integrity and a high caloric response.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is valid for rare-earth-free compositions, with aluminum content not exceeding 10 vol% to avoid significant dilution of the caloric-active phases.
generation.uncertainty: The exact impact of the aluminum binder on the caloric response is uncertain, as it depends on the degree of phase interaction and thermal conductivity changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) the unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and (2) the alloy with 5 vol% aluminum binder. Perform compressive strength tests, caloric response measurements under applied magnetic and pressure fields, and microstructural analysis to assess crack propagation.
measurements: Caloric response (isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change)
Microstructural integrity (e.g., crack density and propagation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the aluminum-modified alloy does not show at least a 50% increase in compressive strength or if the caloric response decreases by more than 10% compared to the unmodified alloy.
